sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
False Creek South is a long-standing example of mixed-tenure housing on public land.

The neighbourhood continues to inform citywide debates about affordability, renewal, and community-led planning.

Residents, co-ops, and local organizations are actively shaping how future redevelopment can protect social mix and long-term stability.

Verified figures are listed in Quick Facts, with linked sources for each value.

highlights.title: Waterfront Public Realm
highlights.description: The seawall and open spaces show how public land decisions shape daily life and access.

highlights.title: Land Trust Direction
highlights.description: Local organizations continue exploring land trust governance as part of future redevelopment.

sections.label: Housing Model
sections.content:
Land Stewardship

Public ownership has supported a mixed-tenure neighbourhood where co-ops, rental housing, and community facilities coexist in close proximity.

Lease Transition

As lease renewals approach, the central policy question is how to maintain affordability while renewing homes and infrastructure.

Community Governance

Residents and housing organizations are advocating for planning approaches that protect social diversity, tenant security, and long-term public benefit.
keyPoints: Public land stewardship shapes local housing outcomes
Mixed tenure supports social diversity and neighbourhood stability
Lease renewal choices will influence future affordability
Community governance remains central to redevelopment planning
Land trust models are active in local policy discussions

sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
Sen̓áḵw is an Indigenous-led rental development on Squamish Nation reserve land.

The project demonstrates how Indigenous jurisdiction can reshape housing delivery, governance, and partnership models in urban settings.

Its design combines market and below-market homes with cultural space and strong transit access.

Verified figures are listed in Quick Facts, with linked sources for each value.

highlights.title: Tower Cluster View
highlights.description: The proposed tower form marks a major shift in scale and rental supply at the south end of Burrard Bridge.

highlights.title: Public Green Space
highlights.description: Open-space planning is integrated with mobility, shoreline access, and cultural gathering.

highlights.title: Transit Connections
highlights.description: The site is tied to major cycling routes, bridge crossings, and regional transit corridors.

highlights.title: Cultural Placekeeping
highlights.description: The project includes Indigenous-led placemaking and community-serving programming.

sections.label: Land Rights
sections.content:
Jurisdiction and Planning

Because the site is on reserve land, development approvals follow Nation and federal frameworks rather than municipal zoning rules.

Partnership Model

Project delivery combines Indigenous leadership with institutional investment while retaining long-term Nation control over land and direction.

Tenant and Community Framework

The rental model prioritizes long-term stewardship, below-market access, and protections aligned with regional tenancy standards.
keyPoints: Indigenous jurisdiction drives planning and governance
The project uses a rental-first stewardship model
Partnership structure supports long-term Nation control
Public access and cultural space are core design priorities

sections.label: Overview
sections.content:
Granville Island is a federal public property known for arts, culture, small business, and food economy activity.

Its governance model relies on land leasing and cross-subsidy, balancing commercial activity with public-serving uses.

Current policy discussion focuses on long-term maintenance, affordability for tenants, and future governance structure.

Verified figures are listed in Quick Facts, with linked sources for each value.

highlights.title: Public Market Core
highlights.description: The market remains a key anchor for food access, tourism, and local business visibility.

highlights.title: Arts and Cultural Tenancy
highlights.description: Leasing policy supports artist spaces and cultural programming alongside commercial uses.

highlights.title: Federal Land Governance
highlights.description: As a federal site, Granville Island follows a distinct planning and management framework.

highlights.title: Future Direction
highlights.description: Stakeholders continue to debate infrastructure renewal, funding pathways, and long-term stewardship options.

sections.label: Land Model
sections.content:
Land Lease Model

Federal ownership and lease management allow the site to support both market activity and mission-driven cultural uses.

Cross-Subsidy Approach

Higher-revenue tenants help sustain lower-rent spaces for artists, non-profits, and public-serving amenities.

Renewal Challenges

Ongoing discussions focus on infrastructure upgrades, tenant affordability, and governance reforms that protect public value.
keyPoints: Federal ownership shapes long-term governance choices
Lease policy balances commercial and cultural uses
Infrastructure renewal is a central strategic challenge
